title: Priya and the Power of Breath
markdown:
Whisperwind smelled of baked bread and banners. The Great Energy Race was coming, a tradition that was not only speed but a sort of cheerful argument about spirit, and Priya — mind as quick as a squirrel at a nut — loved the crowds and the colour and did not love the running. Last year the dusty track had taken her breath the way a startled flock takes off: all at once, and in the wrong direction. Legs heavy. Lungs burning. The finish line performing that trick of moving farther away the harder she tried. She had leaned on the fence afterward, tasting metal, while other children collected their cheers like sweets.

This year the banners were already up, painted with suns that looked a little too confident. Priya practised on the lane behind the bakery and felt the same vanishing. Faster only made the gasp worse and the ache sharper. She sat on the kerb and counted her inhales as if numbers might hold them still. They would not.

Flint the terrier, magnificent of scruff, bounded ahead with a tail like a flag that had never heard of tired. He was a blur of fur and useful barking, the sort of friend who believed a race was a conversation you had with grass. Uncle Dev, imagination as wild as an overgrown garden, offered the usual shoulder-pat: “Chin up, puzzle-solver. The race is not only fast. It is knowing the machine you brought.” Kind. True, probably. And still a piece missing, the way a clock is missing when you have all the cogs and none of the winding.

One bright breezy morning Priya watched Flint chase a sapphire-blue ball across the green. After each sprint he paused, sides heaving like a bellows, pink tongue out, panting in big steady breaths. Not collapsing. Recovering on purpose. Funny. Also interesting, which in Priya’s mind was the better category. She timed one of his pauses against her own leftover stitch from the lane. His pause was work. Hers had been panic wearing running shoes.

Uncle Dev appeared then with a flourish that suggested he had been waiting behind a hedge for the exact moment, carrying a shiny bicycle pump and a deflated bright red balloon. He set them on the bench as if they were instruments.

“Observe.” He pushed air into the balloon. Each regular stroke stretched it bigger, rounder, firmer, a happy bubble with a job. When he stopped, the balloon held its shape. When he let a little air hiss out and pumped again, the lesson sat in the rubber: fill, use, fill. “This air is oxygen. Not a poetic breeze. A useful one. And this biscuit—” a golden treat, held up like evidence “—is fuel. Glucose, if we are being precise. When oxygen and glucose meet inside you, they make the energy for running, jumping, and the sort of thinking that notices a terrier’s bellows.”

Flint, having caught his breath and the smell, thumped the grass with a hopeful tail. Uncle Dev broke the biscuit and gave him a crumb, which Flint accepted as peer review.

“If I pump with no biscuit in the story,” Priya said, “I am only air. If I eat and forget to breathe, I am only crumbs.”

“Exactly. Two parts. One meeting.”

He led them into the dappled Whispering Woods, to a winding path he had named the Energy Track with the confidence of a man who names things and then expects the things to cooperate. Pine needles underfoot. Cool shade that smelled like a cupboard someone had opened on purpose. “A champion knows the breath. Deep one. Fill the balloon.”

Priya drew in cool pine air until a new fullness arrived, lightness with a job. She held it a beat, then let it go without the old gasp. He offered a small honey-sweet apple. “Glucose. Eat it as if you mean the next lap.”

She jogged. The first twenty steps were the old story, legs arguing. Then the inhale arrived on time and the legs, after a brief committee meeting, decided to be springy instead. The old desperate panting gave way to a rhythm: in, useful; out, useful. Flint trotted beside her and copied the deeper breaths, then found an extra spark for butterflies that had not asked to be chased.

They did a second loop. Priya tried the old habit — push, ignore the lungs — and the stitch returned like a rude guest. She stopped, filled the balloon again, and the guest left. Uncle Dev did not say I told you so. He pointed at a mossy stone that marked a third of the track. “That is where last year’s you ran out of coin. This year’s you has a mint.”

“Lungs take the oxygen. Food supplies the glucose. They meet. That meeting is respiration. It is how a body pays for a race without going bankrupt halfway.” He said it once, which was the right number of times. “Not only faster legs. Smarter breath. Wiser fuel.”

Priya felt the last piece click with the particular satisfaction of a puzzle that had been honest all along. She looked at Flint, who wagged as if he had understood the chemistry and merely declined to sit an exam. The Energy Track no longer looked like a mountain. It looked like a place to practise, and practise again tomorrow before the banners got any louder.

On the walk home she made Flint pause after a dash for the sapphire ball and matched her sides to his, bellows to bellows, until the lane behind the bakery felt like woods. She did not wait to be told the world was full of wonders. She logged bellows-pause / pump-and-balloon / apple-on-the-track in her race notebook, pinned a scrap that said oxygen + glucose on the workshop peg, and let Flint carry the ball as if it were a medal he had awarded himself. On race morning she would start with a breath she had already named, eat the apple Uncle Dev had already packed, and treat the first corner as a refill, not a cliff. The banners could do the cheering. Priya would do the inhaling.
